Receiving several offers is good news… that can quickly become stressful. Handled well, a multiple-offer situation maximizes your price and conditions; handled badly, it scares off buyers or creates disputes.
This guide explains how a multiple-offer situation arises, how to compare offers beyond price, and how to decide with method and fairness.
Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page.

Multiple offers are as exciting as they are unsettling. Handled well, they maximize the seller's result; handled badly, they lead to mistakes. This guide explains how they arise, how to compare offers beyond price, the rules to follow and how to decide with method — on BOTH the seller's and the buyer's side.
Multiple offers almost always come from two ingredients: a good (attractive) starting price and a well-prepared, well-distributed property. Scarcity and launch momentum do the rest.
So it's not the product of chance: it's the result of a well-executed price and marketing strategy (see the dedicated guides).

Multiple offers almost always come from two ingredients: a desirable property and a well-calibrated price that creates competition. It's not luck but the result of a good price and marketing strategy.
A fair, even slightly inviting starting price often creates more value than an inflated one: it attracts several buyers and lets competition push the offers up.

Assessing each offer as a whole.
Price, of course — but not only.
Conditions: inspection, financing, document review (fewer conditions = more certainty).
The strength of the buyer's financing (a solid vs uncertain pre-approval).
The deposit and the overall seriousness of the offer.
The highest offer isn't always the best: a slightly lower but near-certain offer can be worth more than a high, fragile one.

Compare each offer as a whole, not just on price: conditions (inspection, financing), dates, deposit, the buyer's strength (pre-approval). A slightly lower offer with no conditions and solid financing can be the safest.
Look at certainty as much as the amount. A high offer conditional on the sale of the buyer's house can collapse; a solid, well-financed offer makes it to the notary.
The rules of the game: fairness and transparency

Handling multiple offers is governed by rules of transparency and fairness toward all buyers. Your broker ensures the process is respected (fair treatment, appropriate communication) to avoid any dispute.
You can accept an offer, refuse it, or make a counter-offer.
The process must stay fair toward all buyers.
Avoid any maneuver that could be perceived as misleading.

Handling multiple offers is governed by rules of fairness and transparency: all buyers must be treated correctly and informed of the process. A misstep can invalidate a transaction or expose you to a complaint — hence the value of a professional framework.
Let your broker steer the process by the rules. Fair, transparent handling protects your sale from challenges — and preserves your reputation.
Choosing the best offer with method.
Choosing the best offer with method.

The euphoria of multiple offers can push you into hasty decisions. Set your priorities in advance (price, dates, certainty), compare coolly, and choose the offer that best serves YOUR goal — not just the biggest number.
Remember: accepting an offer is a commitment. Choose the one most likely to make it to signing.

Euphoria pushes hasty decisions. Set your criteria in advance (price, conditions, acceptable dates), assess coolly, and remember that the best offer is the one that will make it to the notary — not just the highest on paper.
Decide according to your priorities set with a cool head, not in the heat of the bidding. The best offer is the one that meets your goal AND is most likely to succeed.

A solid, serious offer often reassures as much as one more dollar — and protects you from the regret of overpaying.

On the buyer's side, you can stand out without blindly overbidding: arrive pre-approved, offer flexible dates, make a clean offer and set your ceiling in advance. A solid offer often reassures as much as one more dollar — and protects you from the regret of overpaying.
Set your maximum price BEFORE entering a bidding war, and stick to it. Losing a property hurts for a week; overpaying by $30,000 hurts for years. Discipline pays.
